newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain income tax reform to be effective on Jan '99.
newsitem.headline: Spain income tax reform to be effective on Jan '99.

text.p: The Spanish government is working on reforming income tax to reduce fiscal pressure and simplify rules, government officials told Reuters on Friday.
"The (Spanish) Exchequer Secretary Juan Costa created a committee which will present its final results in January 1998, though it could provide some information in advance this fall," she said.
The changes would take effect in January 1999.
The general idea of the reform is to harmonise Spanish fiscal pressure with the lower European levels, allowing a general reduction in Spanish tax rates.
"The highest marginal rate, which now stands at 56 percent, will be reduced at least to 50 percent but all other rates will also be reduced...The reform will affect all levels of income".
In its 1996 electoral campaign, the ruling Popular Party pledged a reduction in income tax, with the intention of bringing the highest rate to 40 percent.
"This will not be possible, at least at the beginning. Because what we have in mind is to keep the public deficit under control," she explained.

She was suggesting that if the economy grew more in subsequent years and the government succeeded in its efforts to keep public expenditures under control further tax reductions could come in the future.

Spanish tax reform must respect an already-approved European convergence plan for 1997-2000 which forecast the deficit over gross domestic product to fall to 2.5 percent in 1998, to 2.0 percent in 1999 and to 1.6 percent in 2000.
The reform will also simplify the system by reducing the number of income brackets to six from ten.

The policy on individual tax deductions will also change. Now deductions are applied on the amount of the tax to be paid, and they are not taken into account before the choice of the income brackets. Under the new system, the deduction will be made before total income is taxed.
"We plan to introduce an entirely new concept on discretionary income, in other words, on the income after expenditures considered necessary for a family to live on," the source said.
These theoretical expenditures will vary depending on the different number of children and other household aspects such as education expenditures.
"This is a very important issue because it will guarantee a fairer system," the source explained.

About the timing of the reform the source said that the study commission would present its result in January. Then the draft, already approved by the cabinet meeting, should be presented to the Parliament in April.
